What is the difference between a container and a virtual machine?

A VM runs a full guest OS on a hypervisor and virtualises hardware, so it is heavy and slow to boot but strongly isolated. A container is an isolated process sharing the host kernel, using namespaces for isolation and cgroups for resource limits. Containers are lightweight, start in seconds and pack densely, but isolation is weaker because the kernel is shared.
What is the difference between an image and a container?

An image is an immutable, layered template containing the filesystem and metadata (entrypoint, env, ports). A container is a running instance of an image with its own writable layer, network and process space. You can start many containers from one image; changes inside a container are lost when it is removed unless stored in a volume.
CMD vs ENTRYPOINT?

ENTRYPOINT defines the executable that always runs; CMD provides default arguments (or a default command if no entrypoint). Arguments passed to docker run image args replace CMD but are appended to ENTRYPOINT; you override the entrypoint only with --entrypoint. Use the exec (JSON array) form so the process is PID 1 and receives SIGTERM for graceful shutdown.
💡 Shell form (CMD java -jar app.jar) wraps the process in /bin/sh -c, which may not forward signals.
COPY vs ADD? RUN vs CMD?

COPY just copies files from the build context; ADD additionally auto-extracts local tar archives and can download URLs, so prefer COPY for predictability. RUN executes at build time and creates a layer (e.g. installing packages); CMD is the default command executed at container start.
How does Docker layer caching work and how do you optimise it?

Each instruction produces a layer; if the instruction and its inputs (files copied, command text) are unchanged, the cached layer is reused, but a change invalidates all subsequent layers. Copy dependency manifests first (pom.xml, package*.json), install dependencies, then copy source code. Add a .dockerignore and combine related RUN commands with cleanup in one step.
What is a multi-stage build and why use it?

A Dockerfile with several FROM stages: earlier stages build the artifact using a full toolchain (Maven + JDK, Node), and the final stage copies only the result (COPY --from=build) onto a slim runtime image. The result is a much smaller image without compilers or source code, which is faster to pull and has fewer vulnerabilities.
How would you containerise an Angular application?

Use a Node stage to run npm ci and ng build, then copy the dist output into an nginx:alpine image. Configure nginx with try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html so client-side routes work on refresh, and add caching headers for hashed assets. Runtime API URLs can be injected via a config JSON loaded at startup or env substitution in nginx templates, since the build output is static.
Volume vs bind mount?

A named volume is managed by Docker under its own storage area, portable across hosts and ideal for database data. A bind mount maps a specific host path into the container; it depends on the host's directory structure and is mainly used in development (live source code, config files). Both survive container removal; data in the container's writable layer does not.
How do containers in Docker Compose talk to each other?

Compose creates a user-defined bridge network for the project, and each service is reachable by its service name via Docker's internal DNS. So the Spring Boot app connects to jdbc:mysql://db:3306/appdb, not localhost – inside a container localhost is the container itself. Port publishing (ports:) is only needed for access from the host.
depends_on doesn't wait for MySQL to be ready. How do you fix it?

Plain depends_on only controls start order. Add a healthcheck to the DB service (e.g. mysqladmin ping) and use depends_on: db: condition: service_healthy. The application should still retry connections (HikariCP/Spring retries, or a startup retry) because in production dependencies can restart at any time.
How do you handle secrets with Docker?

Never put secrets in the Dockerfile via ENV, ARG or copied files – they persist in image layers and history. Inject them at runtime: env vars from an untracked .env for local dev, Docker/Compose secrets mounted under /run/secrets, Kubernetes Secrets, or a cloud secret manager. For build-time credentials (private npm/Maven repos) use BuildKit --mount=type=secret.
A container keeps restarting. How do you debug it?

Check docker ps -a for the exit code and docker logs for the stack trace. docker inspect shows the health status, env and mounts; exit code 137 points to OOM kill, 1 to an application error. Start the image with --entrypoint sh to inspect files and config interactively, or docker exec into it if it stays up long enough.
How do you reduce image size and improve security?

Use multi-stage builds and minimal bases (JRE-only, alpine or distroless), clean package caches in the same RUN, and use .dockerignore. For security: run as non-root with USER, pin image versions, scan with Trivy or Docker Scout, avoid secrets in layers, drop Linux capabilities and use read-only filesystems where possible, and rebuild regularly to pick up base-image patches.
How does the JVM behave inside a container?

Since JDK 10 (backported to 8u191) the JVM is container-aware: it reads cgroup memory and CPU limits rather than host values. By default the max heap is 25% of the container limit, so set -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 or similar. Leave headroom for metaspace, thread stacks and direct buffers, otherwise the kernel OOM-kills the container (exit 137).
What does EXPOSE do? Is it required to publish a port?

EXPOSE is documentation/metadata of the port the application listens on; it does not open anything on the host. Publishing is done at run time with -p hostPort:containerPort (or -P to publish all exposed ports to random host ports). Containers on the same network can reach each other's ports regardless of EXPOSE.
Explain Pod, Deployment and Service in Kubernetes.

A Pod is one or more tightly coupled containers sharing an IP and volumes – the unit Kubernetes schedules. A Deployment manages a ReplicaSet to keep N identical pods running and performs rolling updates and rollbacks. A Service provides a stable virtual IP and DNS name that load-balances across pods selected by labels, since pod IPs change as pods are recreated.
Docker Compose vs Kubernetes?

Compose runs a multi-container app on a single host and is ideal for local development, testing and small deployments. Kubernetes is a cluster orchestrator offering self-healing, horizontal scaling, rolling deployments, service discovery, config/secret management and multi-node scheduling. Many teams use Compose (or Testcontainers) locally and Kubernetes (e.g. GKE) or a serverless container platform (Cloud Run) in production.
How do you tag and push an image to a registry?

Build with a meaningful tag, authenticate, then push:
docker build -t orders:1.4.2 .
docker tag orders:1.4.2 europe-docker.pkg.dev/my-proj/apps/orders:1.4.2
gcloud auth configure-docker europe-docker.pkg.dev
docker push europe-docker.pkg.dev/my-proj/apps/orders:1.4.2
💡 Use immutable tags (version or git SHA) for deployments; latest makes rollbacks and auditing unreliable.
A container exits with code 137. What does it mean?

137 = 128 + 9, so the process received SIGKILL. The most common cause is the out-of-memory killer: the container exceeded its memory limit (docker inspect shows OOMKilled: true; Kubernetes shows reason OOMKilled). For a JVM, check that heap (MaxRAMPercentage) plus metaspace, thread stacks and direct buffers fit the limit. Another cause is docker stop timing out because the app ignored SIGTERM — 143 means it exited on SIGTERM.
docker stop vs docker kill? How do you get graceful shutdown in Spring Boot?

stop sends SIGTERM and, after a grace period (10 s default, -t to change), SIGKILL; kill sends SIGKILL at once. For graceful shutdown the Java process must be PID 1 or receive the signal (exec-form ENTRYPOINT, or --init/tini), and Spring Boot should finish in-flight requests: server.shutdown=graceful with spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase. In Kubernetes, make the grace period (terminationGracePeriodSeconds) longer than the Spring timeout.
What Docker network drivers exist, and how do containers find each other?

bridge (default, single host), host (share the host's network), none, overlay (multi-host) and macvlan. On a user-defined bridge network — which Compose creates automatically — Docker's embedded DNS resolves container/service names, so the app connects to jdbc:mysql://db:3306. The default bridge network has no name resolution. Inside a container, localhost is the container itself, not the host.
What restart policies does Docker support?

no (default), on-failure[:max-retries] (restart only on non-zero exit), always (also restarts when the daemon starts, even after a manual stop) and unless-stopped (like always, but respects a manual stop). In Compose: restart: unless-stopped. In Kubernetes, restarts are handled by the pod's restartPolicy and the controller, with CrashLoopBackOff delays.

Docker vs containerd vs Podman vs OCI?

OCI is the open standard for image format and runtime, so any compliant tool can run any compliant image. containerd is the runtime daemon that manages containers (with runc doing the low-level work); Docker Engine is built on it, and Kubernetes uses containerd or CRI-O directly (dockershim was removed in 1.24). Podman is a daemonless, rootless-friendly CLI compatible with most docker commands. An image built with Docker runs fine on all of them.
How do you build images for both x86 and ARM?

Use docker buildx with --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 and push; the registry stores a multi-platform manifest list and each machine pulls the matching variant. Base images must exist for both architectures (official Temurin, Node and nginx images do). Emulation (QEMU) makes cross-builds slow, so CI often uses native ARM runners. This matters for developers on Apple Silicon and for cheaper ARM cloud instances.
Kubernetes requests vs limits — and why does it matter for Java?

Requests are what the scheduler reserves on a node; limits are the maximum. Exceeding the memory limit kills the pod (OOMKilled); exceeding the CPU limit throttles it, which can slow JVM startup and GC. For Java, set memory request = limit for predictability, size the heap with -XX:MaxRAMPercentage (around 70–75%) to leave room for non-heap memory, and be careful with tight CPU limits on latency-sensitive services.
What is Jib and when would you use it instead of a Dockerfile?

Jib is a Maven/Gradle plugin from Google that builds an OCI image directly from the build, without a Dockerfile or Docker daemon. It separates dependencies, resources and classes into layers automatically, so code changes rebuild only a small layer, and builds are reproducible. Use it to standardise images across many Java services or in CI agents without Docker; use a Dockerfile when you need OS packages or custom setup. Spring Boot's build-image (Buildpacks) is a similar no-Dockerfile option.
ARG vs ENV in a Dockerfile?

| ARG | ENV
Available during build | Yes | Yes (after the ENV line)
Available in the running container | No | Yes
Set from outside | docker build --build-arg | docker run -e, Compose environment
Scope | Ends at the end of its build stage | Inherited by later stages built FROM this one
Safe for secrets | No, visible in image history | No, visible in docker inspect
ARG JAR_FILE=target/app.jar
COPY ${JAR_FILE} app.jar
ENV SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod
Rule of thumb: ARG for build choices such as versions, ENV for runtime defaults that can be overridden. Use BuildKit secret mounts for build secrets and a secret store for runtime ones.
Shell form vs exec form for CMD and ENTRYPOINT?

| Shell form | Exec form
Syntax | CMD java -jar app.jar | CMD ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
Runs as | /bin/sh -c "java -jar app.jar" | java directly
PID 1 | The shell | The JVM
SIGTERM on docker stop | Often not passed to the JVM, so it is killed after the timeout | Reaches the JVM, so graceful shutdown works
Variable expansion ($JAVA_OPTS) | Yes | No (no shell)
Needs a shell in the image | Yes | No (works on distroless)
Rule of thumb: use exec form. If you need variables, use a small script that ends with exec java ..., or let the JVM read JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS itself.
JDK vs JRE vs Alpine vs distroless base image for Spring Boot?

Base | Contains | Pros | Cons
eclipse-temurin:21-jdk | Full JDK on Ubuntu | Compilers and tools; right for the build stage | Large; unneeded at run time
eclipse-temurin:21-jre | JRE only | Smaller, still has a shell for debugging | No jcmd or jstack
*-alpine | musl libc and BusyBox | Very small | musl differences can break native libraries
distroless java | JRE, no shell or package manager | Small attack surface | No shell; harder to debug
Rule of thumb: build with a JDK image in a multi-stage build and run on a JRE or distroless image; choose Alpine only after testing your native dependencies.
Image tag vs image digest: app:latest vs app:1.4.2 vs app@sha256:...?

| :latest | :1.4.2 | @sha256:...
What it is | A default tag name, nothing special | A tag you chose | Hash of the image manifest
Can be moved to another image | Yes | Yes (unless the registry makes tags immutable) | No
Reproducible deploys | No | Mostly | Yes
Human readable | Yes | Yes | No
Rule of thumb: never deploy latest to production. Tag images with a version and commit, enable immutable tags in the registry, and pin digests where you need exact reproducibility.
docker run vs docker exec vs docker attach?

| docker run | docker exec | docker attach
Creates a container | Yes, a new one | No | No
What you get | The container's main process | A new extra process inside a running container | The main process's stdin/stdout
Ctrl+C | Stops the process if attached | Ends only your extra process | Can stop the main process
Typical use | Start a service | docker exec -it app sh to look around | Rarely; watch output of an interactive app
Interview tip: for logs use docker logs -f, not attach. On images without a shell, exec will fail; attach a debug container that shares its namespaces (for example kubectl debug in Kubernetes).
